newsitem.title: MOZAMBIQUE: Mozambique hopes casino will lure rich tourists.
newsitem.headline: Mozambique hopes casino will lure rich tourists.

text.p: The whirr of roulette wheels and the click of dice came to Mozambique on Friday to lure tourists back to the former Portuguese colony over 20 years after Marxists took power.
Maputo's Hotel Polana, restored to its whitewashed and palm-shaded pre-civil war glory, was granted a licence after parliament approved long-banned casinos following lively debate last year.
The hotel on the Indian Ocean hopes the casino in its gracious former dining room will win some of the regional gambling market now dominated by resorts in South Africa and Swaziland.
White South Africans flocked to pre-independence Mozambique in the early 1970s for paradise holidays outside the view of their strictly Calvinist government.

But the tourist industry collapsed after the start of a 16-year civil war between rebels backed by Pretoria and the formerly Marxist Frelimo government that took power on independence from Portugal in 1975.

The country has embraced a market economy since officially abandoning Marxism in 1990 and foreign investment has been picking up. Researchers say Mozambique had the fastest-growing economy in sub-Saharan Africa between 1990 and 1995.
But per capita annual income is still estimated at slightly above $100, making Mozambique's 15 million people among the poorest on the planet.
Rules of the casino permit are tight, apparently intended to confine gambling to tourists and the rich, rather than the locals who might risk their pitiful wages.
City casinos are open only to members or guests of hotels with at least 200 rooms.
Anyone can go to casinos planned in rural resorts, but licences will be granted to resorts or hotels outside cities only if they have a minimum 250 beds.
There are few of these outside Maputo. Much of the countryside is still devastated after the civil war.

The government's Investment Promotion Centre says gaming concessions will be granted only to operators with a minimum $15 million share capital, and they have to pay a once-off fee of $300,000 to set up a casino in existing facilities.
The Casino do Hotel Polana firm said in a statement its $15 million was 40 percent held by Mozambicans and the rest by foreign partners.
The Hotel Polana, the major Mozambican interest in the casino, has 20 percent and South Africa's Karos Hotels, the main shareholder in the hotel itself, holds the same amount.
Mozambique Airlines (LAM) also has shares in the hotel, but there were no details of the other casino investors.
"Non-resident gamblers have the right to transfer abroad their respective gains obtained from their gambling activity in casinos," the Investment Promotion Centre said in a notice.
The state, which still dominates much commercial activity in Mozambique, is not directly involved in gambling but will gain from fees and taxes.
